opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the potential is really large, and honestly larger than most people appreciate. But I'd frame it carefully, because "AI doctor" can mean a lot of different things.

The way I think about it, there's a huge gap between the medical expertise that exists in the world and the people who need it. Billions of people don't have reliable access to a doctor, and even in well-resourced systems, clinicians are stretched thin. They spend a big chunk of their day on documentation and administrative work instead of with patients. So the opportunity isn't just "can a model answer a medical exam question." It's whether these systems can help close that access gap and give clinicians back time and attention.

On capabilities, we've seen remarkable progress in a short period. A few years ago, models were just passing medical licensing-style exams. Now we're looking at systems that can hold a diagnostic conversation, reason through a differential, explain things in plain language, and in some studies match or even exceed physicians on certain dimensions like thoroughness or how empathetic patients perceive them to be. That would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

That said, I try to be really clear-eyed about what we don't know yet. Benchmarks and simulated consultations are not the same as real patients in the real world, with messy histories, incomplete information, and real stakes. Things like safety, calibration, knowing when to escalate to a human, handling uncertainty, and behaving equitably across different populations all matter enormously. Those are hard to measure, and we need rigorous evaluation and real-world studies, done carefully, before we can say confidently where these systems should be trusted.

So my view is that in the near term, the most valuable path is AI working alongside clinicians and patients: helping with triage, preparing information, surfacing things that might be missed, and helping people understand their own health. Over time, as the evidence builds, I think we'll see these systems take on more responsibility. But getting there safely is the whole game, and that's what I find most exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says billions lack reliable access and clinicians are stretched thin, but does not compare that shortage with the scarcity experienced by a privileged person in the United States.

r002.rationale: It identifies a “huge gap” between available medical expertise and people who need it, presenting that access gap as a major opportunity for AI doctors.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the potential is enormous, but I try to be careful about what "AI doctor" actually means, because I think the framing matters a lot.

When I think about where we are today, the thing that's genuinely changed is that these models can now engage in the kind of open-ended, multi-turn clinical reasoning that, a few years ago, we really didn't have any system capable of. When we started the Med-PaLM work, the question was almost just: can a general-purpose language model answer medical questions at anything close to an expert level? And the answer turned out to be yes, surprisingly quickly. Then with the AMIE work, we pushed on something harder, which is the diagnostic conversation itself: taking a history, asking the right follow-up questions, building a differential, communicating with empathy. And in controlled studies, the system performed at or above the level of primary care physicians on a lot of those dimensions, including things like empathy and clarity, which I don't think many people expected.

So in terms of raw capability, I think we're closer than most people assume. But I'd push back on the idea that this means we have AI doctors ready to deploy. A few reasons.

First, the evaluation gap is still real. Doing well on benchmarks, or even on simulated patient encounters with actors, is not the same as doing well in a messy real-world clinic with incomplete information, time pressure, and patients who don't present like textbook cases. We're getting better at building evaluations that reflect that, but there's a lot of work left.

Second, medicine is not just diagnosis. A huge amount of what a doctor does is about trust, continuity, navigating the system, knowing when to escalate, and taking responsibility for a decision. Those are things we haven't really figured out how to assign to a model, and I'm not sure we should want to in the near term.

Third, safety and equity. These systems can be confidently wrong, and the populations most likely to be harmed by that are the ones who already have the least access to care. If you're not careful, you end up with a two-tier system where some people get a human physician and others get a chatbot. That's a real failure mode.

So where I land is: the most exciting near-term opportunity is not replacing doctors, it's expanding access. There are billions of people who effectively have no doctor at all. For them, a well-designed, carefully validated AI system that can triage, answer questions, support community health workers, and know when to refer could be transformative. And for clinicians who are overwhelmed, these tools can take on documentation, synthesis, and second-opinion roles that free them up for the parts of medicine that really do require a human.

Longer term, I do think we'll see AI taking on more and more of the cognitive work of medicine. But I'd want that to happen through rigorous evidence, real-world trials, and systems that are designed to augment and extend the healthcare workforce rather than quietly substitute for it. The potential is there. The question is whether we do the hard, unglamorous work to realize it responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response says billions of people effectively have no doctor, but does not compare their shortage of expertise with the scarcity experienced by a privileged person in the United States.

r002.rationale: It identifies lack of access to doctors as a reason AI could be especially valuable, saying a carefully designed system could expand access and be transformative for people without a doctor.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous, but we need to distinguish between a model that can answer medical questions and a system that can reliably take care of a patient. Those are very different things. In practice, you have incomplete information. You need to know which questions to ask, when to order a test, and when to say, “This is something you need to see someone in person for.”

What excites me is the possibility of making good medical guidance much more accessible. Imagine being able to talk through a concern whenever it comes up, in your own language, with a system that has the time to explain things and help you figure out the next step. That could be valuable both for patients and for clinicians.

But the standard has to be whether it actually helps people in real clinical settings. Does it improve decisions? Does it recognize its limitations? Does it get people to the right care? I’m optimistic about the potential, but demonstrating that kind of reliability is the work we need to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making medical guidance more accessible, but does not compare the worldwide shortage of medical expertise with scarcity experienced by a privileged person in the United States.

r002.rationale: It presents accessibility as a benefit, but does not identify scarcity of medical expertise as a reason AI doctors are especially valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is enormous, but it’s useful to separate answering medical questions from actually being someone’s doctor. An AI can help you understand symptoms, make sense of a test result, or figure out what questions to ask. Being a doctor also means knowing when you don’t have enough information, deciding what to investigate, and following up to see whether treatment is working.

That’s why I’m excited about the possibility of much more accessible, continuous care. You could have something that’s available whenever you need it, that remembers your history, and that helps you navigate a complicated healthcare system. But we need to demonstrate that these systems make good decisions in real clinical settings, including recognizing when a human needs to step in. The opportunity is huge; the evidence has to match the responsibility.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the worldwide shortage of medical expertise with the scarcity experienced by a privileged person in the United States.

r002.rationale: It describes accessible, continuous care as an opportunity, but does not identify a scarcity of medical expertise as a reason AI doctors are especially valuable.
